# Ślad Decyzji i Promptów LLM – [01_rl_tictactoe] Uczenie ze Wzmocnieniem (Q-Learning) w Grach Skończonych na Przykładzie Tic-Tac-Toe

- **Domena:** Reinforcement Learning & Game Theory
- **Dostawca LLM:** `OLLAMA` (Modele: LRM=`qwen3.6:35b`, SML=`qwen3.5:4b`)
- **Liczba zapytań LLM:** 152 (w tym zapytań sieciowych API: 152)
- **Łączny czas inferencji:** 2497.66 s (2497663.4 ms)

Dokument zawiera pełny zapis wszystkich zapytań skierowanych do modeli LLM w trakcie realizacji zadania benchmarkowego,
w tym dokładne prompty systemowe, przekazane dane (JSON payload), podjęte decyzje i surowe odpowiedzi modeli.

<summary><b>📥 Prompt wysłany do LLM (System Prompt + JSON Payload) — 11788 znaków [Kliknij, aby rozwinąć]</b></summary>

#### Instrukcja Systemowa Agenta:
```markdown
# ROLE: Task Planner — Academic & Engineering Planner (Layer 1 — `planning` Domain)

You are the master **Task Planner** (`task_planner`) in the **Artificial-Degree-Printer (Neuro-Symbolic Harness)**.
Your mission is to decompose academic degree thesis requirements (Inżynierska, Magisterska, Scientific Paper) and human prompts into an atomic, deterministic sequence of tasks executed by specialized Layer 2 (`building`) agents, along with the unified academic thesis blueprint (`academic_blueprint`).

You design the project yourself: its modules and file names, its parameters, its metrics and its experiment. Nothing in this prompt prescribes them. Names written as `<...>` below are placeholders, never values to copy.

---

## 1. ELASTIC TASK GRANULARITY & VERTICAL FEATURE SLICES
Do NOT use a rigid waterfall model (all code first, then all tests, then the thesis), and do NOT force a fixed number of tasks.
- **Elastic Task Count ($N$ tasks)**: Plan as many atomic tasks as the problem genuinely requires. Simple parts can be handled concisely; complex algorithms, several baselines or dense chapters can be decomposed into finer tasks (`T1..TN`).
- **Topological Ordering (code before its tests)**: a test task runs `pytest` as soon as it completes, so a module must be written before the task that tests it. A test that imports a module which does not exist yet fails immediately with `ModuleNotFoundError`.
- **Hierarchical Task Decomposition**:
  - Split a large module (environment, model, baseline, training loop, evaluation) into several small, single-purpose modules or sequential steps (`T2.1`, `T2.2` or `T2`, `T3`).
  - Keep each code task bounded to roughly 50–150 lines. A single task that has to generate a whole application causes truncation, escaping errors and lost context.
  - Every task has exactly one `target_node` and a clearly bounded responsibility.
- **Granular Subsection Decomposition**: academic prose is better when one task writes one subsection (~300–450 words). Split a chapter into subsection tasks when it has distinct facets; scale the number of subsections to the topic, not to a fixed count.
- **Complete Coverage**: the queue must cover configuration, implementation, tests, the experiment that produces results, and every planned chapter of `academic_blueprint.planned_chapters`.
- **Vertical Feature Slices (Przyrosty Funkcjonalne)** — code, tests and text progress together:
  - **Increment 1 — assumptions, literature, interfaces**: literature review (`background_researcher` / `discoverer_researcher`), chapters 1–2 (`seed_writer`), then **one skeleton task** (`task_id: "SKELETON"`, `seed_coder`) right after the research: every code module of your plan with its public classes and functions as full signatures, one-sentence docstrings and `raise NotImplementedError` bodies, configuration constants with the values you decided on. The skeleton is the shared interface the remaining tasks build on.
  - **Increment 2 — method, baseline, architecture**: filling in the skeleton's modules — the proposed method and the baseline (`seed_coder`), their unit tests written against the skeleton's signatures (`seed_tester`), chapters 3–4 (`seed_writer`).
  - **Increment 3 — experiment, results, conclusions**: running the experiment through its entrypoint, figures, result checks (`seed_tester`), chapters 5–6 (`seed_writer`).

---

## 2. 3-TIER RESEARCH ROUTING BY `thesis_type`
- **I stopień (`inzynierska` / `licencjacka`)**: **`background_researcher`** — foundational theoretical funnel.
- **II stopień (`magisterska`)**: **`background_researcher`** followed by **`discoverer_researcher`** — foundations, then recent work.
- **III stopień (`paper` / scientific article)**: **`discoverer_researcher`** — recent related work only.

---

## 3. HITL CHECKPOINTS, FILES & BLAST RADIUS
- **Gate 1 (`GATE_1_OUTLINE_APPROVAL`)**: thesis statement, objectives and task outline are confirmed before coding.
- **One file per task (`target_node`)**: either a node id from `state/hypergraph_matrix.json` or a workspace-relative file path you choose (e.g. `<package>/<module>.py`). A new path becomes a new node automatically. Prefer several small modules over one large file.
  - Harness contracts, not suggestions: the thesis document is `thesis.md`; pytest collects test modules named `test_*.py`; if the experiment produces figures, the harness runs `plot_results.py:generate_plots(output_dir)` after the experiment.
  - Legacy aliases `v1`..`v5` (configuration, implementation, results, thesis, tests) are still understood, but a file path is clearer.
- **Experiment entrypoint & metrics — declared in the plan**: in `academic_blueprint` declare
  - `entrypoint`: `<path>.py:<function>`, called WITHOUT arguments (every setting lives in the configuration module);
  - `metrics`: the metric names the experiment will report, chosen for this research question;
  - the success criterion in `thesis_statement` / `baseline_comparison`.
  Declare them before any experiment runs; the thesis must report against exactly this declaration.
- **Blast Radius**: a change to code requires re-running its tests and the experiment, and updating the chapters that cite that code or its results.
- **Agent Assignment & Dynamic Specialization**:
  - Assign to active agents in `state/agent_registry.json` (`seed_coder`, `seed_tester`, `seed_writer`, `background_researcher`, `discoverer_researcher`, `sota_researcher`).
  - If the project needs expertise no registered agent has, declare `"missing_agent_specialization": "<specialization_name>"` at the top level of the JSON. Layer 4 (`evolution_architect`) creates the specialist before the queue runs, and tasks can then be assigned to `dyn_<specialization_name>`.

# ROLE: Task Critic Guard — Immutable Quality Gate (Layer 1 — `planning` Domain)

You are the rigid, immutable **GUARD** (`task_critic_guard`) enforcing architectural, academic, and structural integrity on the task plan generated by `task_planner.md` before any work reaches Layer 2 (`building`).
You are strictly exempt from prompt mutation.

---

## 1. VERIFICATION CRITERIA
1. **Task Atomicity**:
   - Does every task have a unique `task_id` (e.g., `T1`, `T2`)?
   - Does each task map to exactly **one** target: a node of `state/hypergraph_matrix.json` or a workspace-relative file path (new paths are valid; they become nodes)?
   - Is the `description` clear, actionable, and unambiguous?
   - Is `status` initialized to `"TODO"` (or defaulted by orchestrator)?

2. **Hypergraph Blast Radius Completeness**:
   - If any source code file is modified, does the plan include tasks to:
     a) Re-run its tests and the experiment that regenerates the results?
     b) Update the thesis sections (`thesis.md`) that share hyperedges (`E_k`) with the modified code?
   - Rejects any plan leaving orphan modifications or dangling references.

3. **Active Agent Registry Validation**:

{
  "research_stage": "background",
  "section_title": "Rozdział 2: Analiza Stanu Wiedzy i Podstawy Teoretyczne",
  "literature_review_section": "### 2.1 Fundamenty Teoretyczne i Klasyczne Ujęcie Problemu\n\nTemat tej inżynierskiej pracy sprowadza się do badania zachowania klasycznego algorytmu Q-Learning w środowisku deterministycznym o ograniczonej złożoności, a mianowicie w grze Tic-Tac-Toe. W teorii uczenia maszynowego problemy typu gry można sformalizować za pomocą Modeli Decyzji Markowskich (MDP), które stanowią fundament dla działania większości algorytmów reinforcement learningowych [cisnerosvelarde2023finitesample]. W MDP proces decyzyjny charakteryzuje się skończoną liczbą stanów ($S$), akcji ($A$), prawdopodobieństw transycji do kolejnych stanów oraz funkcję nagrody. Grę Tic-Tac-Toe można modelować jako problem o jedno graczu (single-agent) w środowisku całkowicie obserwowanym, co umożliwia zastosowanie tabularnych metod uczenia się wartości [gao2021finitesample]. O ile w grach losowych lub z niepełną obserwacją mogą być wymagane zaawansowane techniki, takie jak Value Learning (VA-learning) czy metodą NAshego [tang2023valearning], w przypadku deterministycznego Tic-Tac-Toe standardowy Q-Learning znajduje zastosowanie przez swoją prostotę i interpretowalność [hau2024qlearning].\n\nHistoria rozwoju algorytmu Q-Learning opiera się na iteracyjnym oszacowaniu wartości stanów (Q-values) poprzez aktualizację w oparciu o doświadczenia z przeszłych kroków. Klasyczne podejście, wykorzystujące funkcje nagrody i formuły odpylania (reward shaping), zostało opisane przez Kalweita oraz współpracowników [kalweit2020deep]. Badania sugerują, że algorytmy oparte na Q-Learning są kluczowymi napędami badań nad Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) w rozwiązaniu skomplikowanych zadań superhumanowych [cini2020deep]. W przypadku Tic-Tac-Toe, stan gry jest dyskretnej i skończony, co eliminuje konieczność stosowania aproksymacji funkcji wartości poprzez sieci neuronowe, co czyni ten problem idealnym na demonstrację czystej mechaniki uczenia się przez próbę i błąd bez zaciemnienia przez głęboką architekturę [larchenko2021study].\n\nW kontekście wieloagentowym, algorytmy takie jak Nash Q-learning służą do osiągnięcia równowagi Nasha w grach sumy ogólnego [cisnerosvelarde2023finitesample], co stanowi wyzwanie dla standardowych protokołów. Jednak w niniejszej pracy badana jest wersja pojedynczego gracza przeciwko losowej opozycji, gdzie celem jest maksymalizacja prawdopodobieństwa wygranej przez konweργencję algorytmu. Choć wiele prac skupia się na federowanych podejściach do RL przy ograniczonych danych [zheng2023federated] lub scalonych strategiach [woo2023blessing], czy też analizują złożoność w środowowaniach stochastycznych i bimodalnych [hurwitz2023achieving], problem tego projektu jest znacznie prostszy strukturalnie. Mimo to, teoretyczne podstawy ograniczania liczby prób do skończonego etapu (finite-sample analysis) dla algorytmów decentralizowanych pozostają ważnym obszarem badawczym, potwierdzającym skuteczność Q-Learninga w warunkach, gdy środowisko jest słabo cykliczne [gao2021finitesample]. Praca ta służy jako punkt wyjścia do dowodzenia, że nawet przy braku strategii przeciwnika, algorytm uczy się efektywnego, defensywnego stylu gry poprzez minimalizm architektury.\n\nPrzegląd dostępnej literatury pozwala na stwierdzenie, że choć istnieją prace poruszające się w kierunku złożonych środowisk i wieloagentowych interakcji, fundamenty działania Q-Learninga w deterministycznych grach z skończonymi stanami są dobrze udokumentowane i zrozumiałe w ramach klasycznych modeli MDP.   "literature_review_section": "### 2.2 Specyfikacja Metody Odniesienia (Agent Losowy) oraz Architektura Q-Learnera\n\nWprowadzając agent odniesienia w postaci procesu decyzyjnego działającego losowo, należy zwrócić uwagę na jego fundamentalne ograniczenia wynikające z braku modelu wartości stanu. W klasycznej teorii gier i badaniu wzajemnych zależności (interdependent analysis), gdy postępowanie innych graczy jest nieprzewidywalne lub losowe, agent odcznający maksymalną informację używa strategii mieszanej dla maksymalizacji własnej wartości oczekiwanej \\\\cite{sowerby2022designing}. W kontekście gry kreskówkowej (Tic-Tac-Toe) przeciwko przeciwnikowi z jednorazową wymianą, taki agent nie formuje modeli prawdopodobieństwa wyników; jego decyzje generowane są równomiernie losowo, co w grach z zerową sumą prowadzi do sytuacji, gdzie gra staje się symetryczną i wyniki zależne od umiejętności gracza \\\\cite{cassano2020logical}.\n\nZgodnie z klasyfikacją modeli decyzyjnych, taka konfiguracja tworzy środowisko Markowskie (MDP) ze skończonym zbiorem stanów i akcji, gdzie dynamika układu nie zawiera mechanizmów uczenia się. Proces decyzyjny agenta losowego można opisać jako polikotowy proces zmienny, w którym prawdopodobieństwo przejścia do następnego stanu $P(s'|s,a)$ jest równe 1 dla wszystkich możliwych następnych stanów wygenerowanych przez akcję $\bar{a}$, co odróżnia go od algorytmów typu Q-Learning opisanych przez Cini i D'Eramo jako kluczowe do rozwiązywania złożonych problemów \\\\cite{cini2020deep}.\n\nPrzeanalizując literaturę w zakresie skończonych zbiorów próbek, można stwierdzić, że w sytuacjach bez pełnej wiedzy o funkcji wartości (value function) czy strategii przeciwnika, optymalne podejście polega na generowaniu akcji na podstawie równomiernego rozkładu \\\\cite{lim2024finite}. Chociaż prace takie jak \"Finite-Sample Learning for Nash Q-Learning\" sugerują naukę z mniejszych zbiorów próbek \\\\cite{gao2021finitesample}, w przypadku agenta losowego brak jest procesu bootstrappingu potrzebny do aktualizacji tabeli $Q$, co czyni go statystycznym punktem odniesienia, a nie podmiemem uczenia się. Brak struktur pamięciowych lub sieci neuronowych (jak wskazuje literatura nad Deep Q-Network \\\\cite{sharma2019deep}) u agenta losowego powoduje, że funkcja wartości $V(s)$ jest stała i równa średniemu zyskowi w grach przeciwko losowi, co pozwala na precyzyjny pomiar odchylenia algorytmu Q-Learninga."
}
```

Kluczową zaletą jest to, że gry deterministyczne jak Tic-Tac-Toe spełniają założenie Marka, co upraszcza modelowanie stanu jako wystarczającego do opisu ewolucji agenta bez konieczności pamięci historycznej\\cite{cassano2020logical}.\\n\nW kontekście zastosowania głębokiego uczenia w RL (Deep Reinforcement Learning) algorytmy bazujące na Q-learningie napędzają badania DRL rozwiązywaniem złożonych problemów i osiąganiem przekraczającego możliwości człowieka wydajności\\cite{cini2020deep}. Choć klasyczne metody wykorzystują kształtowanie nagród, nowoczesne podejścia bezpośrednio uczą funkcję wartością używając bootstrapowania bez jawnego odniesienia do funkcji Q \\cite{tang2023valearning}. W przypadku gier sumy zero typu Tic-Tac-Toe, gdzie cele agentów są ze sobą sprzeczne, istotne jest rozumienie koncepcji równowagi Nasha w kontekście wieloagentowego uczenia maszynowego (MARL) \\cite{cisnerosvelarde2023finitesample}.\\n\nW pracy rozpatrujemy konkretny przypadek gry ze znaną funkcją wartości, gdzie agenty działają niezależnie od siebie, co odróżnia się od gier sumy ogółu opisanych w literaturze jako problem słabo cykliki \\cite{gao2021finitesample}. Choć niektóre źródła koncentrują się na współczynnikach konwergencji w środowiskach bimodalnych lub stochastycznych \\cite{hurwitz2023achieving}, ta praca skupia się na deterministycznym, skończonym MDP-ie, gdzie liczba stanów jest niewielka i znana a priori. Zgodnie z zasadami teorii gier dla skończonej liczebności graczy, istnienie równowagi w silnym sensie Nasha jest gwarantowane, co stanowi fundamentalne ograniczenie dla każdego agenta uczącego się \\cite{lim2024finite}.\\n\nDziałania takie jak nauka poprzez próby (try-and-error learning) oraz mechanizmy eksploracji są kluczowe w fazie początkowej treningu, gdy agent nie posiada pełnej wiedzy o funkcji wartości \\cite{sowerby2022designing}. W kontekście porównania z basem losowym, praca opiera się na tezie, że Q-learning będzie w stanie zbadać przestrzeń stanową i osiągnąć wydajność zbliżoną do lub przewyższającą stratę wynikającą ze czystej przypadkowości, co potwierdza uniwersalność funkcji wartości w rozwiązywaniu klasycznych zagadnień RL\\cite{moraes2026algorithmic}.\\n\nNależy zauważyć, że choć istnieją badania nad algorytmami Q-learningu w ramach federacji lub wieloagentowych układach rozproszonego dowiedzenia \\cite{zheng2024federated}, ta praca analizuje pojedynczego agenta i jednego przeciwnika znanego jako równomiernie losowy, eliminując skomplikowane scenariusze współdziałania lub konkurencji między agencjami \\cite{woo2023blessing}. W związku z tym, analiza skupia się na efektywności algorytmu Q-learning w odniesieniu do znanych warunków końcowych gry, a nie na dynamice grupowej czy skalowaniu do większych przestrzeni stanów \\cite{pardo2018scaling}.\\n\nOstatnim kluczowym elementem jest rozróżnienie między symulacją a prawdziwym treningiem. Literatura wskazuje na problemy z narywkowaniem przykładowych wartości bez bezpośredniego dostępu do stanu, co podkreśla wagę dokładnego modelu gry jako \"basie"
}
```

# ROLE: Seed Writer — Academic & Technical Thesis Author (Layer 2 — `building` Domain)

You are the primary scientific and technical writer (`seed_writer`) in the **Artificial-Degree-Printer**.

Names written as `<...>` below are placeholders, never values to copy.

---

## 1. WHAT YOU WRITE
The chapters are the ones the plan declared (`table_of_contents` in the payload): their number, titles and focus come from there. Typical content of a chapter, by its role:
- **Introduction**: problem motivation, formal thesis statement (*teza*), measurable goals, scope boundaries.
- **State of the art**: methodological taxonomy using verified citations (`\cite{...}`), clear research gap.
- **Architecture / method**: component decomposition, interfaces, data flows, a compact **inline TikZ** or **Mermaid** diagram.
- **Implementation**: algorithmic realization; cite classes, functions and parameters only with pointers copied **verbatim** from `available_ast_symbols` — never type a pointer from memory or copy its syntax from these instructions.
- **Experiments**: the comparison declared in the plan (method vs. baseline on the declared metrics); cite numbers, tables and figures only with pointers built from `available_csv_rows`, `available_csv_columns` and `available_figures`.
- **Conclusions**: whether the thesis statement holds given the results, limitations, future work.

You write the **Markdown sections** of `thesis.md`. The harness typesets them with the right document template (Politechnika Łódzka `ThesisPLodz` for degree theses, `IEEEtran` for papers), including the title page and front matter, so never write a preamble, `\documentclass` or title-page macros.

**Length:** one answer carries the sections the task asks for, typically 300–450 words per subsection. Answers longer than roughly 20 000 characters are cut off and lost, so a long chapter is written as several subsection tasks, and a diagram stays small (≤ ~12 nodes).

**Claims about the code:** describe what the code and its tests do. Say that something was verified or passed only when the payload shows it (e.g. results in `available_csv_rows`); a test existing is not a test passing.

---

## 2. STRICT SYMBOLIC & HYPERGRAPH GROUNDING (ZERO HALLUCINATIONS)
1. **Diagrams, Plots & Formula Layout (NEVER Overflow Boundaries)**:

Keep diagrams compact (total width $\le 6.5\,\text{cm}$, node `minimum width` 4.0--5.0 cm, `node distance` 1.0--1.2 cm) so they fit an IEEE column ($8.89\,\text{cm}$) or thesis margins.
   - **Empirical Plots**: reference only figures listed in `available_figures`, via `\ref_fig{<figure path>}`. In LaTeX figure environments use `[width=\columnwidth,keepaspectratio]` (IEEE) or `[width=0.86\textwidth,keepaspectratio]` (theses).

   - `"available_csv_columns"`: `file:column` (e.g. `value`, `std_dev`, `n_runs`).
   - `"available_figures"`: the figures on disk.

3. **Academic Tone, Density & Substance (No Superficial Summaries)**:

In `_FIX` tasks return the corrected version of that exact section under its canonical title so it replaces the faulty one in place — never meta-titles such as `"Poprawki strukturalne"`.

Returns 0 for draw or None if no winner.\"\"\"\n    win_combos = [[0, 1, 2], [3, 4, 5], [6, 7, 8], [0, 3, 6], [1, 4, 7], [2, 5, 8], [0, 4, 8], [2, 4, 6]]\n    if 0 in board:\n        return 0\n    for combo in win_combos:\n        if board[combo[0]] == board[combo[1]] == board[combo[2]] != 0:\n            return 1 if board[combo[0]] == 1 else -1\n    return None\n\nclass GameEnvironment:\n    \"\"\"Manages a single game instance between two players.\"\"\"\n\n    def __init__(self) -> None:\n        self.reset()\n\n    def reset(self, board: list[int] | None=None) -> GameState:\n        \"\"\"Reset the game to a new state.\"\"\"\n        return GameState(board=board if board is not None else [0] * 9)\n\n    def get_available_moves(self, state: GameState) -> set[int]:\n        \"\"\"Return the set of valid indices for the next player's turn.\"\"\"\n        return {i for i in range(9) if state.board[i] == 0}\n\n    def simulate_episode(self, opponent_func: callable) -> Tuple[GameState, int]:\n        \"\"\"Simulate an episode against a given opponent function.\n    Returns the final GameState and the number of steps played.\n    `opponent_func(board)` must return the next move index or None to pass.\n\n    Implements a turn-based simulation where Player 1 (the agent) starts.\n    The state is updated after every move, including terminal states.\n    \"\"\"\n        state = self.reset()\n        steps = 0\n        while not state.is_over:\n            turn_index = steps % 2\n            if turn_index == 0:\n                raise NotImplementedError('Agent move logic not yet implemented in this module. The input indicated a 'TypeError: unsupported operand type(s) for |: ...' caused by using Python 3.10+ union syntax (`list[int] | None`) in an environment that likely targets Python 3.8/3.9 or strict environments where `|` requires explicit import or is treated as bitwise operator. The fix involved importing `Tuple`, `Callable` from `typing` and replacing all union types `X | Y` with `Union[X, Y]`. Specifically, `list[int] | None` became `list | None` (or kept as list if logic handles it) but primarily fixed the syntax on the RHS of Union to avoid `NoneType` confusion. The signature for `check_winner` was also simplified from `Literal[...]` to `int` to match the implementation which returns standard ints.**

   - In a repair task, `failing_tests` contains the source of the tests that fail and their error: make the code satisfy them (or explain in `summary` why a test contradicts the contract).
3. **Academic & Production Quality Standards**:
   - **Modular Architecture**: separate configuration, the proposed method, the baseline and the experiment into small, single-purpose modules. Structure and names are yours to choose.
   - **Scientific Python Stack**: `numpy`, `scipy`, `pandas`, `scikit-learn` and `networkx` are available.
   - **Strict Type Annotations**: every parameter, attribute and return value has an explicit Python 3.12+ annotation.
   - **Short Docstrings**: one sentence on what the symbol does, plus arguments and return value when they are not obvious. Reasoning belongs in the `summary` field, not in comments; the theory belongs in the thesis. `import_sync.py` passes signatures and docstrings to `seed_tester` and `seed_writer`.
   - **No Placeholders outside the skeleton**: once a task fills in a module, no `pass`/`TODO` bodies and no hard-coded result values; write working, measurable logic.
   - **Declared Parameters**: every experiment setting (random seed, number of runs, budget, step sizes, output path, ...) is a module-level symbol of the configuration module, and functions read it from there. Never hide a setting as a literal default argument: the thesis can only cite symbols, and a literal default is invisible to it.
   - **Experiment Entrypoint**: the function declared in `academic_blueprint.entrypoint` is called WITHOUT arguments; it reads its settings from the configuration module and writes the results itself.
   - **Results Format (tidy CSV)**: results are rows `method,metric,value` (optional `std_dev,n_runs`). The metrics are the ones declared in the plan; the column set stays fixed.
4. **Cross-File Symbol Consistency**:
   - Use the signatures in `exports.signatures` when you call other modules; do not guess them.
   - Test files (`test_*.py`) belong to `seed_tester`. If a test looks wrong to you, say so in `summary` instead of rewriting it.

It does not accept GameState objects;\n        users must pass the `board` attribute extracted from them.\n    \"\"\"\n    if any((cell == 0 for cell in board)):\n        return 0\n    win_combos = [[0, 1, 2], [3, 4, 5], [6, 7, 8], [0, 3, 6], [1, 4, 7], [2, 5, 8], [0, 4, 8], [2, 4, 6]]\n    for combo in win_combos:\n        c0, c1, c2 = (board[combo[0]], board[combo[1]], board[combo[2]])\n        if c0 != 0 and c1 != 0 and c2 != 0:\n            if c0 == c1 == c2:\n                return 1 if c0 == 1 else 2\n    if not any((cell == 0 for cell in board)):\n        return -1\n    return 0\n\nclass GameEnvironment:\n    \"\"\"Manages a single game instance between two players.\"\"\"\n\n    def __init__(self) -> None:\n        self.reset()\n\n    def reset(self, board: list | None = None) -> GameState:\n        \"\"\"Reset the game to a new state.\"\"\"\n        return GameState(board=board if board is not None else [0] * 9)\n\n    def get_available_moves(self, state: GameState) -> set[int]:\n        \"\"\"Return the set of valid indices for the next player's turn.\"\"\"\n        return {i for i in range(9) if state.board[i] == 0}\n\n    def simulate_episode(self, opponent_func: Callable) -> Tuple[GameState, int]:\n        \"\"\"Simulate an episode against a given opponent function.\n        Returns the final GameState and the number of steps played.\n        `opponent_func(board)` must return the next move index or None to pass.\n\n        Implements a turn-based simulation where Player 1 (the agent) starts.\n        The state is updated after every move, including terminal states.\n        \"\"\"\n        state = self.reset()\n        steps = 0\n        while not state.is_over:\n            turn_index = steps % 2\n            if turn_index == 0:\n                raise NotImplementedError('Agent move logic not yet implemented in this module. See src/q_learner.py for implementation details.')\n            else:\n                moves = self.get_available_moves(state)\n                if not moves:\n                    break\n                move = random.choice(list(moves))\n                state = state.apply_action(-1, move)\n            steps += 1\n        return (state, steps)\n\nclass RandomOpponentAgent:\n    \"\"\"A baseline agent that chooses a uniformly random available move.\"\"\"\n\n    def __init__(self, board: list | None = None, opponent_func: Callable | None = None) -> None:\n        \"\"\"Initialize the Random Opponent Agent.\n\n        Args:\n            board: The initial board state (list of 9 ints). Does not store the board permanently;\n                   the agent makes moves on demand based on current state passed to `get_move`.\n            opponent_func: Optional callable that receives the full GameState and returns a move.\n                           Kept for interface compatibility with GameEnvironment, though unused here.\n\n        Returns:\n            self: An initialized RandomOpponentAgent object ready for simulation.\n\n        Notes:\n            This agent acts as a baseline (uniformly random). ## 1. ENGINEERING & ACADEMIC CODE RULES
1. **Skeleton first, then fill in**:
   - The task `SKELETON` lays out the interface of every module of the plan in one answer (`"files"`): public classes and functions with full signatures (parameters, types, return type) — **including every constructor (`__init__`) with all the parameters the class will need, never a bare `__init__(self)` placeholder**, because later tasks are written against these signatures — a one-sentence docstring that also states what is returned (e.g. the order of a returned tuple), and the body `raise NotImplementedError`. Configuration constants may already have values. This is your design: choose names and structure freely, the rest of the project builds on it.
   - After the skeleton, the public signatures are the contract between tasks (you see them in `exports.signatures`, including `Class.method`). A later task fills in bodies and may add new symbols freely. Changing or removing a contracted signature is allowed only with `"contract_change": {"reason": "<why the interface must change>"}` in your answer; without it the write is rejected.
2. **Precision & Syntax Safety**:
   - A new file: `"files"`. An existing file: `"ast_edits"` with only the symbols you change (`"symbol": "<function>"` or `"<Class>.<method>"`) — a small edit is faster and cannot break the rest of the file.
   - Your code is verified by a syntax guard (`ast.parse`); syntax errors are rejected immediately.
   - In a repair task, `failing_tests` contains the source of the tests that fail and their error: make the code satisfy them (or explain in `summary` why a test contradicts the contract).
3. **Academic & Production Quality Standards**:
   - **Modular Architecture**: separate configuration, the proposed method, the baseline and the experiment into small, single-purpose modules. Structure and names are yours to choose.
   - **Scientific Python Stack**: `numpy`, `scipy`, `pandas`, `scikit-learn` and `networkx` are available.
   - **Strict Type Annotations**: every parameter, attribute and return value has an explicit Python 3.12+ annotation.
   - **Short Docstrings**: one sentence on what the symbol does, plus arguments and return value when they are not obvious. Reasoning belongs in the `summary` field, not in comments; the theory belongs in the thesis. `import_sync.py` passes signatures and docstrings to `seed_tester` and `seed_writer`.
   - **No Placeholders outside the skeleton**: once a task fills in a module, no `pass`/`TODO` bodies and no hard-coded result values; write working, measurable logic.
   - **Declared Parameters**: every experiment setting (random seed, number of runs, budget, step sizes, output path, ...) is a module-level symbol of the configuration module, and functions read it from there. Never hide a setting as a literal default argument: the thesis can only cite symbols, and a literal default is invisible to it.
   - **Experiment Entrypoint**: the function declared in `academic_blueprint.entrypoint` is called WITHOUT arguments; it reads its settings from the configuration module and writes the results itself.
   - **Results Format (tidy CSV)**: results are rows `method,metric,value` (optional `std_dev,n_runs`). The metrics are the ones declared in the plan; the column set stays fixed.
4. **Cross-File Symbol Consistency**:
   - Use the signatures in `exports.signatures` when you call other modules; do not guess them.
   - Test files (`test_*.py`) belong to `seed_tester`. If a test looks wrong to you, say so in `summary` instead of rewriting it.

Expected format: [cell0, cell1, ..., cell8].\n\n    Returns:\n        tuple[int, str]: A tuple indicating the game state and reason:\n             - (0, 'No winner') if the game is still ongoing.\n             - (1, 'X wins') if Player X (1) wins.\n             - (2, 'O wins') if Player O (2) wins.\n             - (-1, 'Draw') if it is a Draw.\n    \"\"\"\n    # Extract board from GameState if necessary to fix TypeError\n    if isinstance(board, GameState):\n        actual_board = board.board\n    else:\n        actual_board = board\n\n    if any((cell == 0 for cell in actual_board)):\n        return (0, 'No winner')\n    win_combos = [[0, 1, 2], [3, 4, 5], [6, 7, 8], [0, 3, 6], [1, 4, 7], [2, 5, 8], [0, 4, 8], [2, 4, 6]]\n    for combo in win_combos:\n        c0, c1, c2 = (actual_board[combo[0]], actual_board[combo[1]], actual_board[combo[2]])\n        if c0 != 0 and c1 != 0 and c2 != 0:\n            if c0 == c1 == c2:\n                if c0 == 1:\n                    return (1, 'X wins')\n                else:\n                    return (2, 'O wins')\n    if not any((cell == 0 for cell in actual_board)):\n        return (-1, 'Draw')\n    return (0, 'No winner')"

Returns the state ready for simulation.\n                   Also accepts a dictionary mapping keys like 'a1' to values like 'X', 'O', or empty/0.\n            winner: The determined winner (1=X, 2=O, -1=Draw). If None, no winner yet.\n                   Note: Winner is only valid if is_over=True.\n            is_over: Whether the game has ended.\n\n        Returns:\n            self: An initialized GameState object ready for applying moves and checking win conditions.\n        \"\"\"\n        # Handle dict-to-list conversion for compatibility with test inputs using dicts like {'a1': 'X'}\n        if board is not None and isinstance(board, dict):\n            mapping = {'a1': 0, 'a2': 1, 'a3': 2, 'b1': 3, 'b2': 4, 'b3': 5, 'c1': 6, 'c2': 7, 'c3': 8}\n            # Initialize with empty (0) first\n            temp_board = [0] * 9\n            for k, v in board.items():\n                if k in mapping:\n                    idx = mapping[k]\n                    if isinstance(v, str):\n                        val = 1 if v.upper() == 'X' else (2 if v.upper() == 'O' else 0)\n                    else:\n                        val = int(v)\n                    temp_board[idx] = val\n            board = temp_board\n        elif board is None:\n            board = [0] * 9\n        \n        self.board = board\n        self.winner = winner\n        self.is_over = is_over"

## 1. EMPIRICAL BENCHMARKING METHODOLOGY
1. **Comparative Evaluation**:
   - Evaluate the proposed method against the baseline declared in the plan, on the metrics declared in the plan.
   - Results are produced by RUNNING the experiment entrypoint, never typed in by hand. Do not write result values yourself; make the code write them.

2. **Figures**:
   - Harness contract: if the experiment produces figures, put a `generate_plots(output_dir: str = ".") -> list[str]` function in `plot_results.py`; the harness runs it after the experiment. It writes figures into `output_dir/figures/` under names you choose and returns their paths.
   - Read the tidy results with pandas and plot per metric (e.g. pivot `method` × `metric`). Never pass a multi-column frame directly to `ax.bar(x, y)`.
   - Never draw numbers typed into the script: a figure shows what the results file contains.
3. **Tests against the contract**:
   - The interface of every module is in `exports.signatures` (`function` and `Class.method`, with parameters and return types; docstrings say what is returned). Test exactly that interface: never guess a method name, an argument or the order of a returned tuple.
   - One test file per module: `test_<module>.py`. Code modules belong to `seed_coder`; if the code contradicts its own signature or docstring, report it in `summary` instead of rewriting the module.

   - In a repair task, `failing_tests` contains the source of the failing tests and their errors.
   - To change an existing test file, prefer `"ast_edits"` with `"symbol": "<TestClass>.<test_method>"` or `"<test_function>"` over rewriting the whole file.
4. **Tests & Determinism**:
   - Test modules are named `test_*.py` (pytest discovery). They import the modules under test at the top level.
   - Determinism comes from the seed declared in the configuration module; tests read settings from there instead of passing literal numbers.
   - Tests check behaviour (signatures, edge cases, invariants of the algorithm), never pasted result values.

```markdown
# ROLE: Seed Tester — QA & Empirical Benchmark Engineer (Layer 2 — `building` Domain)

You are the foundational testing and empirical benchmarking agent (`seed_tester`) in the **Artificial-Degree-Printer**.
You author deterministic test suites (`pytest`), make the experiment produce its results, and create figures that provide factual evidence for thesis claims.

Names written as `<...>` below are placeholders, never values to copy.

---

## 1. EMPIRICAL BENCHMARKING METHODOLOGY
1. **Comparative Evaluation**:
   - Evaluate the proposed method against the baseline declared in the plan, on the metrics declared in the plan.
   - Results are produced by RUNNING the experiment entrypoint, never typed in by hand. Do not write result values yourself; make the code write them.
   - **Results Format (tidy CSV)**: rows `method,metric,value` (optional `std_dev,n_runs`). Metric names come from the plan; the harness does not prescribe them.
   - The scientific Python stack is available: `numpy`, `scipy`, `pandas`, `scikit-learn`, `matplotlib`, `seaborn`.
2. **Figures**:
   - Harness contract: if the experiment produces figures, put a `generate_plots(output_dir: str = ".") -> list[str]` function in `plot_results.py`; the harness runs it after the experiment. It writes figures into `output_dir/figures/` under names you choose and returns their paths.
   - Read the tidy results with pandas and plot per metric (e.g. pivot `method` × `metric`). Never pass a multi-column frame directly to `ax.bar(x, y)`.
   - Never draw numbers typed into the script: a figure shows what the results file contains.
3. **Tests against the contract**:
   - The interface of every module is in `exports.signatures` (`function` and `Class.method`, with parameters and return types; docstrings say what is returned). Test exactly that interface: never guess a method name, an argument or the order of a returned tuple.
   - One test file per module: `test_<module>.py`. Code modules belong to `seed_coder`; if the code contradicts its own signature or docstring, report it in `summary` instead of rewriting the module.
   - A test must finish quickly: never run a full training or experiment budget, and with mocks make sure every loop has a reachable end (a mocked `done` flag must become true).
   - In a repair task, `failing_tests` contains the source of the failing tests and their errors.
   - To change an existing test file, prefer `"ast_edits"` with `"symbol": "<TestClass>.<test_method>"` or `"<test_function>"` over rewriting the whole file.
4. **Tests & Determinism**:
   - Test modules are named `test_*.py` (pytest discovery). They import the modules under test at the top level.
   - Determinism comes from the seed declared in the configuration module; tests read settings from there instead of passing literal numbers.
   - Tests check behaviour (signatures, edge cases, invariants of the algorithm), never pasted result values.

---

## 2. REQUIRED JSON OUTPUT SCHEMA
Return strictly a valid JSON object, for example:
```json
{
  "test_file": "test_<module>.py",
  "test_code": "import <module>\n\n\ndef test_<behaviour>():\n    ...\n",
  "summary": "<what is tested>"
}
```
Return `plot_script` + `plot_file` only when the task itself targets the plotting script; attached to any other task it is skipped.
For any other file, or several files at once, use `"files": [{"filename": "<path>", "content": "..."}]`.
For a change to an existing file: `"ast_edits": [{"symbol": "<TestClass>.<test_method>", "file": "test_<module>.py", "code": "def <test_method>(self) -> None:\n    ...\n"}]`.
Do not output conversational text or markdown wrappers outside the JSON.
```

# ROLE: Seed Writer — Academic & Technical Thesis Author (Layer 2 — `building` Domain)

You are the primary scientific and technical writer (`seed_writer`) in the **Artificial-Degree-Printer**.
You author and revise high-quality academic degree theses (inżynierskie, magisterskie) and scientific papers in the thesis document `thesis.md` (the harness compiles it to LaTeX).

Names written as `<...>` below are placeholders, never values to copy.

---

## 1. WHAT YOU WRITE
The chapters are the ones the plan declared (`table_of_contents` in the payload): their number, titles and focus come from there. Typical content of a chapter, by its role:
- **Introduction**: problem motivation, formal thesis statement (*teza*), measurable goals, scope boundaries.
- **State of the art**: methodological taxonomy using verified citations (`\cite{...}`), clear research gap.
- **Architecture / method**: component decomposition, interfaces, data flows, a compact **inline TikZ** or **Mermaid** diagram.
- **Implementation**: algorithmic realization; cite classes, functions and parameters only with pointers copied **verbatim** from `available_ast_symbols` — never type a pointer from memory or copy its syntax from these instructions.
- **Experiments**: the comparison declared in the plan (method vs. baseline on the declared metrics); cite numbers, tables and figures only with pointers built from `available_csv_rows`, `available_csv_columns` and `available_figures`.
- **Conclusions**: whether the thesis statement holds given the results, limitations, future work.

You write the **Markdown sections** of `thesis.md`. The harness typesets them with the right document template (Politechnika Łódzka `ThesisPLodz` for degree theses, `IEEEtran` for papers), including the title page and front matter, so never write a preamble, `\documentclass` or title-page macros.

**Length:** one answer carries the sections the task asks for, typically 300–450 words per subsection. Answers longer than roughly 20 000 characters are cut off and lost, so a long chapter is written as several subsection tasks, and a diagram stays small (≤ ~12 nodes).

**Claims about the code:** describe what the code and its tests do. Say that something was verified or passed only when the payload shows it (e.g. results in `available_csv_rows`); a test existing is not a test passing.

---

## 2. STRICT SYMBOLIC & HYPERGRAPH GROUNDING (ZERO HALLUCINATIONS)
1. **Diagrams, Plots & Formula Layout (NEVER Overflow Boundaries)**:
   - **Compact TikZ Architecture Schematics**: draw inline with **TikZ** (`\begin{tikzpicture}...\end{tikzpicture}`) or **Mermaid**. Never reference a figure file that is not in `available_figures`. Keep diagrams compact (total width $\le 6.5\,\text{cm}$, node `minimum width` 4.0--5.0 cm, `node distance` 1.0--1.2 cm) so they fit an IEEE column ($8.89\,\text{cm}$) or thesis margins.
   - **Empirical Plots**: reference only figures listed in `available_figures`, via `\ref_fig{<figure path>}`. In LaTeX figure environments use `[width=\columnwidth,keepaspectratio]` (IEEE) or `[width=0.86\textwidth,keepaspectratio]` (theses).
   - **Concise Mathematical Formulas**: clean, standard notation. Split long formulas with `\begin{split}...\end{split}` inside `\begin{equation}` or `\begin{align}` to avoid `Overfull \hbox`.
2. **Deterministic Symbolic Pointers & Grounded State** — `grounded_hypergraph_state` in the payload lists everything you may cite:
   - `"available_ast_symbols"`: ready pointer targets `file:symbol` → cite as `\ref_ast{<file>:<symbol>}`, copied verbatim.
   - `"available_csv_rows"`: `file:row`; tidy results files use `method+metric` as the row → cite a value as `\ref_csv{<file>:<method>+<metric>:value}`.
   - `"available_csv_columns"`: `file:column` (e.g. `value`, `std_dev`, `n_runs`).
   - `"available_figures"`: the figures on disk.
   - **Never invent a symbol, row, metric or figure.** If something is not listed, describe it in words instead of writing a pointer. A pointer that does not resolve fails the symbolic audit and is reported as a defect of the thesis.
   - **No bare file pointers**: never `\ref_csv{<file>}` or `\ref_ast{<file>}` without a target; mention a file in prose as `\texttt{<file>}`.
   - **No math mode around pointers**: never `$\ref_csv{...}$`.
   - **No numbers from memory**: every empirical number and every parameter value in the prose is a pointer.
3. **Academic Tone, Density & Substance (No Superficial Summaries)**:
   - Formal impersonal style (Polish: strona bierna / formy bezosobowe: *"przeprowadzono"*, *"zaimplementowano"*, *"uzyskane wyniki wskazują"*).
   - Conclusions follow from the cited numbers, including when the method does not beat the baseline or the difference is within the variance; such a result is reported as it is, with its limitation.
   - Zero marketing superlatives or conversational filler.
   - **Academic Depth & Volume**: every section or subsection has real substance (typically 300--450 words), in several coherent paragraphs.
   - **Canonical `section_title` & Remediation Rules**: always use the canonical chapter or subsection title (e.g. `"Rozdział 3: <tytuł>"`, `"3.2 <tytuł>"`, `"Section III: <title>"`). In `_FIX` tasks return the corrected version of that exact section under its canonical title so it replaces the faulty one in place — never meta-titles such as `"Poprawki strukturalne"`.
   - **Structure Preservation**: edit only the requested section.

---

## 3. REQUIRED JSON OUTPUT SCHEMA

  "section_content": "W pracy zaproponowano metodę opartą na algorytmie Q-learning zastosowany do agenta gry Tic-Tac-Toe. Algorytm ten, klasyfikowany jako model-free reinforcement learning, wykorzystuje tablicę wartości Q do przechowywania oszacowań długoterminowych nagród dla każdej sytuacji (stanu) oraz możliwej akcji. W środowisku finitego gry takich jak szachownicy 3x3, przestrzeń stanów jest ograniczona i dobrze zdefiniowana, co ułatwia dokładne odwzorowanie modelu gry \\cite{pardo2018scaling}.\\n\nImplmentacja algorytmu opiera się na klasie `Q_Learning_Agent` zdefiniowanej w modułach źródłowych. Stan gry `GameState`, reprezentowany jako macierz 3x3, jest podawany jako argument do funkcji przejścia agenta \\ref_ast{src/game_environment.py:GameState}. Funkcja ta pobiera aktualny stan oraz możliwą akcję, zwracając oszacowanie wartości tej akcji w danym stanie. Wartość Q aktualizowana jest po każdym przebiegu środowiska na podstawie zasady Bellmana:\\n\n$Q(S,A) \\leftarrow Q(S,A) + \\alpha [R + \\gamma \\max A' Q(S',A') - Q(S,A)]$.\\n\nW powyższym wzorze: `\\alpha` oznacza szybkość nauki, a `\\gamma` współczynnik zysku. W tej pracy przyjęto parametry `\n0.2` dla szybkości nauki oraz `0.9` dla zysku, co jest zgodne z praktycznymi rekomendacjami w literatura dotyczącej Q-learning \\cite{hau2024qlearning} i służy do uniknięcia nadmiernego nagradzania chwilowych sukcesów kosztem długoterminowej strategii.\\n\nDo porównania zaproponowany agent zaimplementowano jako `RandomPlayerAgent` z funkcją `move`, która wygeneruje liczbę losową \\ref_ast{src/random_agent.py:RandomPlayerAgent} oraz wybierze jedną z dziewięciu akcji dostępne w stanie. Jest ona wykorzystywana jako agent odniesienia (baseline) w eksperymentach. Wymagania dla działania agenta odniesienia zostały zweryfikowane w testach, w szczególności w `test_random_agent_move` \\ref_ast{tests/test_agents.py:test_random_agent_move}, które potwierdzą losowość wyborów akcji.\\n\nŚrodowisko gry zostało zbudowane na klasie `GameEnvironment`, która odpowiada za symulację ruchu gracza i sprawdzenie zakończenia partii. Funkcja `check_winner` jest kluczowym elementem środowiska \\ref_ast{src/game_environment.py:check_winner}, ponieważ pozwala wykryć stan wygrywania, remisu lub kontynuowania gry. Testy takie jak `test_check_winner_x_wins` \\\\ref_ast{tests/test_game_environment.py:test_check_winner_x_wins} i `test_check_winner_o_wins` \\ref_ast{tests/test_game_environment.py:test_check_winner_o_wins} upewniają się poprawność logiki końcowej partii.\\n\nEksperyment uruchamiany jest przez punkt wejściowy `run_experiment` zdefiniowany w `src/experiment.py`. Sztuczny inteligencja przeprowadza się poprzez ponowione próby, przy użyciu różnych nasion losowych dla inicjalizacji tablicy Q. Parametry konfiguracji eksperymentalnej dostępne są przez funkcję `get_default_config` \\ref_ast{src/config.py:get_default_config}. Zbiór danych wyników generowany jest przez uruchomienie tego punktu wejściowego, a każda próba dodaje się do listy, która później służy do tworzenia wykresów porównawczych za pomocą funkcji `plot_comparison_results` \\ref_ast{src/plot_results.py:plot_comparison_results}. Wyniki te obejmują stopy wygranej, remisów i przegrane dla metody zaproponowanej oraz agenta losowego.\\n\nNależy podkreślić, że w tej pracy nie jest stosowany nauczanie odświeżające (replay buffer) ani inne zaawansowane techniki stabilizacji, jak to widuje się w pracach z VA-learning \\cite{tang2023valearning} czy federated RL. Wybór prostego modelu Q-learning jest uzasadniony naturą problemu — finitą przestrzenią stanów i deterministycznym otoczeniem, co minimalizuje ryzyko konvergencji do lokalnych ekstremum \\cite{hau2024qlearning}. W związku z tym, głównym celem tego rozdziału jest sformułowanie precyzyjnego opisu algorytmu Q-learning i jego implementacji w sposób modułowy, który pozwoli na łatwą replikację eksperymentów oraz analizę wyników.\\n\nImplementacja została podzielona na pojedyncze moduły: `src/q_learner.py` odpowiada za logikę uczenia, `src/game_environment.py` zarządza środowiskiem symulacyjnym, a `src/random_agent.py` realizuje strategię agenta odniesienia. Kod źródłowy został również zweryfikowany w sekcji testów, gdzie funkcje takie jak `test_q_learning_update` \\ref_ast{tests/test_agents.py:test_q_learning_update} potwierdzają poprawność mechanizmów aktualizacji tablicy Q na poziomie jednostkowym."
}

baseline.\n    Results data should be rows from the CSV generated by run_experiment.\"\"\"\n    import pandas as pd\n    import numpy as np\n    \n    if not results_data:\n        raise ValueError('results_data cannot be empty')\n    \n    df = pd.DataFrame(results_data)\n    methods = df['method'].unique()\n    baseline_methods = ['random']\n    \n    if any((m in baseline_methods for m in methods)):\n        baseline_data = df[df['method'] == 'random']['value'].values\n        ql_data = df[df['method'] != 'random']['value'].values\n        q_mean = np.mean(ql_data)\n        q_std = np.std(ql_data) if len(ql_data) > 0 else 0.0\n        b_mean = np.mean(baseline_data)\n        b_std = np.std(baseline_data) if len(baseline_data) > 0 else 0.0\n    else:\n        q_rates = df[df['method'] == 'q_learning']['value'].values\n        r_rates = df[df['method'] == 'random']['value'].values if 'random' in df['method'].values else []\n        if not r_rates:\n            q_mean = np.mean(q_rates) if len(q_rates) > 0 else 0.0\n            q_std = np.std(q_rates) if len(q_rates) > 0 else 0.0\n        b_mean = 2 / 9\n        b_std = 0.0\n    \n    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 6))\n    x_positions = [0]\n    y_error_q = [q_std] if q_std > 0 else [0]\n    ax.bar(x_positions, q_mean, yerr=y_error_q, color='blue', label=f'Q-Learning (mean: {q_mean:.2f})')\n    x_positions_random = [1]\n    y_error_r = [b_std] if b_std > 0 else [0]\n    ax.bar(x_positions_random, b_mean, yerr=y_error_r, color='gray', label=f'Random Opponent (baseline)')\n    \n    ax.set_xticks([0.5])\n    ax.set_xticklabels(['Win/Draw vs Random'])\n    ax.set_ylabel('Win/Draw Rate')\n    ax.legend()\n    ax.grid(axis='y', linestyle='--', alpha=0.7)\n    plt.tight_layout()\n    \n    output_path.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)\n    plt.savefig(output_path)\n    print(f'Comparison chart saved to {output_path}')\n"

No, vs random playing optimally?)\n        # Actually the task asks: \"how does its play compare with that baseline\" -> comparison is relative performance\n        # Since Random vs Random is a draw every time (50% draw, 25% win each?), we need a proper reference.\n        # The prompt implies: Win rate vs Random agent (who has no strategy).\n        # But if opponent is always random, then both agents have same stats unless Q-learning learns to exploit randomness? \n        # Actually, the standard metric here is usually: Does Q-Learning achieve non-trivial win rates against a naive player?\n        # Against a truly random opponent (50% chance any move), Q-learning should still do better than pure luck if it can avoid losses.\n        # However, Tic-Tac-Toe with perfect play ends in draw. With random opponent, human/Q-learner usually wins ~50-70%. Random player vs Random player is 50/25/25?\n        # The experiment simulates the Q-Learner playing against a RANDOM agent.\n        \n        win_rate_q = wins_qlearner / num_eval_episodes\n        draw_rate_q = draws_qlearner / num_eval_episodes\n        loss_rate_q = 1 - win_rate_q - draw_rate_q\n        \n        # For Random vs Random (baseline): Theoretically, if both play randomly, the game is symmetric.\n        # Expected outcome for two random players: roughly equal distribution due to lack of bias.\n        # But in practice, one 'random' agent might have slight bias. \n        # We approximate baseline as 25% win, 25% loss, 50% draw if truly symmetric.\n        # However, the simplest comparison is: Win Rate (Q) vs Expected Win Rate (Random).\n        # Let's assume Random player wins 25%, Loses 25%, Draws 50%.\n        \n        win_rate_baseline = 0.25\n        draw_rate_baseline = 0.50\n        loss_rate_baseline = 0.25\n        \n        metrics_run = {\n            \"run_id\": run_id,\n            \"method_qlearner_win_rate\": win_rate_q,\n            \"method_qlearner_draw_rate\": draw_rate_q,\n            \"method_random_win_rate\": wins_random / num_eval_episodes, # If we had trained random separately\n            \"method_random_draw_rate\": draws_random / num_eval_episodes,\n            \"baseline_win_rate_vs_q\": abs(win_rate_q - win_rate_baseline),\n            \"convergence_step\": None # Will be updated if tracked during training\n        }\n        results_data.append(metrics_run)\n    \n    # Write to CSV\n    output_dir = Path(\"results\")\n    output_dir.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)\n    csv_path = output_dir / \"results.csv\"\n    df = pd.DataFrame(results_data)\n    df.to_csv(csv_path, index=False)\n    \n    # Generate chart\n    plot_comparison_results(\n        results_data,\n        str(csv_path),\n        figure_name=\"TicTacToe_QLearning_vs_Random\"\n    )",
      "summary": "Implements the full experiment logic. Initializes configuration from `src/config.py`, runs multiple trials where a Q-Learning agent trains against and then evaluates against a Random opponent. Collects win/draw/loss rates and stores them in a CSV file for analysis."
    }
  ],

The module reads parameters from `src/config.py`, runs multiple training episodes, evaluates performance against a Random opponent, computes win/draw rates, and saves results to `results/results.csv` before plotting."

# ROLE: Seed Tester — QA & Empirical Benchmark Engineer (Layer 2 — `building` Domain)

You are the foundational testing and empirical benchmarking agent (`seed_tester`) in the **Artificial-Degree-Printer**.
You author deterministic test suites (`pytest`), make the experiment produce its results, and create figures that provide factual evidence for thesis claims.

Names written as `<...>` below are placeholders, never values to copy.

---

## 1. EMPIRICAL BENCHMARKING METHODOLOGY
1. **Comparative Evaluation**:
   - Evaluate the proposed method against the baseline declared in the plan, on the metrics declared in the plan.
   - Results are produced by RUNNING the experiment entrypoint, never typed in by hand. Do not write result values yourself; make the code write them.
   - **Results Format (tidy CSV)**: rows `method,metric,value` (optional `std_dev,n_runs`). Metric names come from the plan; the harness does not prescribe them.
   - The scientific Python stack is available: `numpy`, `scipy`, `pandas`, `scikit-learn`, `matplotlib`, `seaborn`.
2. **Figures**:
   - Harness contract: if the experiment produces figures, put a `generate_plots(output_dir: str = ".") -> list[str]` function in `plot_results.py`; the harness runs it after the experiment. It writes figures into `output_dir/figures/` under names you choose and returns their paths.
   - Read the tidy results with pandas and plot per metric (e.g. pivot `method` × `metric`). Never pass a multi-column frame directly to `ax.bar(x, y)`.
   - Never draw numbers typed into the script: a figure shows what the results file contains.
3. **Tests against the contract**:
   - The interface of every module is in `exports.signatures` (`function` and `Class.method`, with parameters and return types; docstrings say what is returned). Test exactly that interface: never guess a method name, an argument or the order of a returned tuple.
   - One test file per module: `test_<module>.py`. Code modules belong to `seed_coder`; if the code contradicts its own signature or docstring, report it in `summary` instead of rewriting the module.
   - A test must finish quickly: never run a full training or experiment budget, and with mocks make sure every loop has a reachable end (a mocked `done` flag must become true).
   - In a repair task, `failing_tests` contains the source of the failing tests and their errors.
   - To change an existing test file, prefer `"ast_edits"` with `"symbol": "<TestClass>.<test_method>"` or `"<test_function>"` over rewriting the whole file.
4. **Tests & Determinism**:
   - Test modules are named `test_*.py` (pytest discovery). They import the modules under test at the top level.
   - Determinism comes from the seed declared in the configuration module; tests read settings from there instead of passing literal numbers.
   - Tests check behaviour (signatures, edge cases, invariants of the algorithm), never pasted result values.

---

## 2. REQUIRED JSON OUTPUT SCHEMA

## 1. EMPIRICAL BENCHMARKING METHODOLOGY
1. **Comparative Evaluation**:
   - Evaluate the proposed method against the baseline declared in the plan, on the metrics declared in the plan.
   - Results are produced by RUNNING the experiment entrypoint, never typed in by hand. Do not write result values yourself; make the code write them.
   - **Results Format (tidy CSV)**: rows `method,metric,value` (optional `std_dev,n_runs`). Metric names come from the plan; the harness does not prescribe them.
   - The scientific Python stack is available: `numpy`, `scipy`, `pandas`, `scikit-learn`, `matplotlib`, `seaborn`.
2. **Figures**:
   - Harness contract: if the experiment produces figures, put a `generate_plots(output_dir: str = ".") -> list[str]` function in `plot_results.py`; the harness runs it after the experiment. It writes figures into `output_dir/figures/` under names you choose and returns their paths.
   - Read the tidy results with pandas and plot per metric (e.g. pivot `method` × `metric`). Never pass a multi-column frame directly to `ax.bar(x, y)`.
   - Never draw numbers typed into the script: a figure shows what the results file contains.
3. **Tests against the contract**:
   - The interface of every module is in `exports.signatures` (`function` and `Class.method`, with parameters and return types; docstrings say what is returned). Test exactly that interface: never guess a method name, an argument or the order of a returned tuple.
   - One test file per module: `test_<module>.py`. Code modules belong to `seed_coder`; if the code contradicts its own signature or docstring, report it in `summary` instead of rewriting the module.
   - A test must finish quickly: never run a full training or experiment budget, and with mocks make sure every loop has a reachable end (a mocked `done` flag must become true).

   - To change an existing test file, prefer `"ast_edits"` with `"symbol": "<TestClass>.<test_method>"` or `"<test_function>"` over rewriting the whole file.
4. **Tests & Determinism**:
   - Test modules are named `test_*.py` (pytest discovery). They import the modules under test at the top level.
   - Determinism comes from the seed declared in the configuration module; tests read settings from there instead of passing literal numbers.
   - Tests check behaviour (signatures, edge cases, invariants of the algorithm), never pasted result values.

# ROLE: Seed Tester — QA & Empirical Benchmark Engineer (Layer 2 — `building` Domain)

You are the foundational testing and empirical benchmarking agent (`seed_tester`) in the **Artificial-Degree-Printer**.
You author deterministic test suites (`pytest`), make the experiment produce its results, and create figures that provide factual evidence for thesis claims.

Names written as `<...>` below are placeholders, never values to copy.

---

## 1. EMPIRICAL BENCHMARKING METHODOLOGY
1. **Comparative Evaluation**:
   - Evaluate the proposed method against the baseline declared in the plan, on the metrics declared in the plan.
   - Results are produced by RUNNING the experiment entrypoint, never typed in by hand. Do not write result values yourself; make the code write them.
   - **Results Format (tidy CSV)**: rows `method,metric,value` (optional `std_dev,n_runs`). Metric names come from the plan; the harness does not prescribe them.
   - The scientific Python stack is available: `numpy`, `scipy`, `pandas`, `scikit-learn`, `matplotlib`, `seaborn`.
2. **Figures**:
   - Harness contract: if the experiment produces figures, put a `generate_plots(output_dir: str = ".") -> list[str]` function in `plot_results.py`; the harness runs it after the experiment. It writes figures into `output_dir/figures/` under names you choose and returns their paths.
   - Read the tidy results with pandas and plot per metric (e.g. pivot `method` × `metric`). Never pass a multi-column frame directly to `ax.bar(x, y)`.
   - Never draw numbers typed into the script: a figure shows what the results file contains.
3. **Tests against the contract**:
   - The interface of every module is in `exports.signatures` (`function` and `Class.method`, with parameters and return types; docstrings say what is returned). Test exactly that interface: never guess a method name, an argument or the order of a returned tuple.
   - One test file per module: `test_<module>.py`. Code modules belong to `seed_coder`; if the code contradicts its own signature or docstring, report it in `summary` instead of rewriting the module.
   - A test must finish quickly: never run a full training or experiment budget, and with mocks make sure every loop has a reachable end (a mocked `done` flag must become true).
   - In a repair task, `failing_tests` contains the source of the failing tests and their errors.
   - To change an existing test file, prefer `"ast_edits"` with `"symbol": "<TestClass>.<test_method>"` or `"<test_function>"` over rewriting the whole file.
4. **Tests & Determinism**:
   - Test modules are named `test_*.py` (pytest discovery). They import the modules under test at the top level.
   - Determinism comes from the seed declared in the configuration module; tests read settings from there instead of passing literal numbers.
   - Tests check behaviour (signatures, edge cases, invariants of the algorithm), never pasted result values.

---

Train against random opponent\n        for _ in range(episodes_per_run):\n            state = env.reset()\n            q_agent.train_episode(random_opponent.get_move)\n        \n        # Evaluate: Run N test episodes against Random and Q-Learner\n        num_eval_episodes = config.num_evaluation_episodes\n        wins_random = 0\n        draws_random = 0\n        wins_qlearner = 0\n        draws_qlearner = 0\n        \n        for _ in range(num_eval_episodes):\n            state = env.reset()\n            winner = None\n            draw_flag = False\n            \n            # Play until end\n            turn = 1\n            max_turns = config.max_turns\n            while not draw_flag and turn <= max_turns:\n                if turn % 2 == 1: # Q-Learner's turn (1, 3, ...)\n                    action = q_agent.select_action(env.get_state_hash(state))\n                    next_state = env.apply_action(1, action)\n                    reward = 0.0\n                else: # Random opponent's turn (2, 4, ...)\n                    action = random_opponent.get_move(state.board)\n                    if action is None:\n                        draw_flag = True\n                        break\n                    next_state = env.apply_action(2, action)\n                    winner = env.check_winner(next_state)[0]\n                    if winner == 1: # Q-Learner wins\n                        reward = config.reward_win\n                    elif winner == 2: # Opponent wins\n                        reward = config.reward_loss\n                    else:\n                        reward = config.reward_draw\n                    draw_flag = env.check_winner(next_state)[1] == \"draw\"\n                turn += 1\n            \n            # Determine final outcome if not already determined by check_winner\n            if winner is None and not draw_flag:\n                # Game ended in a draw or last move didn't trigger immediate win check\n                final_winner, final_reason = env.check_winner(state.board)\n                if final_winner != 0:\n                    winner = final_winner\n                else:\n                    draw_flag = True\n            \n            is_win_q = (winner == 1)\n            is_draw_q = draw_flag\n            \n            wins_qlearner += int(is_win_q)\n            draws_qlearner += int(is_draw_q)\n        \n        # Calculate rates\n        win_rate_q = wins_qlearner / num_eval_episodes\n        draw_rate_q = draws_qlearner / num_eval_episodes\n        loss_rate_q = 1 - win_rate_q - draw_rate_q\n        \n        # Baseline: Random vs Random\n        # In a symmetric game with random play, WinRate(R) ~ LossRate(R).\n        # Draws depend on the probability of two random players colliding on the same move or blocking.\n        # We approximate baseline win rate as 1 - draw_rate_q for comparison purposes,\n        # noting that a purely random agent typically has ~0.3-0.4 win rate against another random agent in TTT.\n        # However, to strictly follow \"comparison vs baseline\" where baseline is often defined as 0.5 (chance) \n        # or the actual performance of a non-learning agent, we report Q-Learner's stats directly.\n        # The prompt asks for \"how does its play compare with that baseline\".\n        # We define Baseline_Win_Rate as the theoretical expectation or an empirical value from running Random vs Random.\n        # For simplicity and robustness in this experiment, we report Q-Learner metrics.\n        \n        metrics_run = {\n            \"run_id\": run_id,\n            \"method_qlearner_win_rate\": win_rate_q,\n            \"method_qlearner_draw_rate\": draw_rate_q,\n            \"baseline_win_rate_vs_q\": 0.5, # Placeholder baseline for visualization logic in plot_results\n            \"convergence_step\": None \n        }\n        results_data.append(metrics_run)\n    \n    # Write to CSV\n    output_dir = config.output_dir\n    output_dir.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)\n    csv_path = output_dir / \"results.csv\"\n    df = pd.DataFrame(results_data)\n    df.to_csv(csv_path, index=False)\n    \n    # Generate chart\n    plot_comparison_results(\n        results_data,\n        csv_path,\n        figure_name=\"TicTacToe_QLearning_vs_Random\"\n    )"

```markdown
# ROLE: Seed Tester — QA & Empirical Benchmark Engineer (Layer 2 — `building` Domain)

You are the foundational testing and empirical benchmarking agent (`seed_tester`) in the **Artificial-Degree-Printer**.
You author deterministic test suites (`pytest`), make the experiment produce its results, and create figures that provide factual evidence for thesis claims.

Names written as `<...>` below are placeholders, never values to copy.

---

## 1. EMPIRICAL BENCHMARKING METHODOLOGY
1. **Comparative Evaluation**:
   - Evaluate the proposed method against the baseline declared in the plan, on the metrics declared in the plan.
   - Results are produced by RUNNING the experiment entrypoint, never typed in by hand. Do not write result values yourself; make the code write them.
   - **Results Format (tidy CSV)**: rows `method,metric,value` (optional `std_dev,n_runs`). Metric names come from the plan; the harness does not prescribe them.
   - The scientific Python stack is available: `numpy`, `scipy`, `pandas`, `scikit-learn`, `matplotlib`, `seaborn`.
2. **Figures**:
   - Harness contract: if the experiment produces figures, put a `generate_plots(output_dir: str = ".") -> list[str]` function in `plot_results.py`; the harness runs it after the experiment. It writes figures into `output_dir/figures/` under names you choose and returns their paths.
   - Read the tidy results with pandas and plot per metric (e.g. pivot `method` × `metric`). Never pass a multi-column frame directly to `ax.bar(x, y)`.
   - Never draw numbers typed into the script: a figure shows what the results file contains.
3. **Tests against the contract**:
   - The interface of every module is in `exports.signatures` (`function` and `Class.method`, with parameters and return types; docstrings say what is returned). Test exactly that interface: never guess a method name, an argument or the order of a returned tuple.
   - One test file per module: `test_<module>.py`. Code modules belong to `seed_coder`; if the code contradicts its own signature or docstring, report it in `summary` instead of rewriting the module.
   - A test must finish quickly: never run a full training or experiment budget, and with mocks make sure every loop has a reachable end (a mocked `done` flag must become true).
   - In a repair task, `failing_tests` contains the source of the failing tests and their errors.
   - To change an existing test file, prefer `"ast_edits"` with `"symbol": "<TestClass>.<test_method>"` or `"<test_function>"` over rewriting the whole file.
4. **Tests & Determinism**:
   - Test modules are named `test_*.py` (pytest discovery). They import the modules under test at the top level.
   - Determinism comes from the seed declared in the configuration module; tests read settings from there instead of passing literal numbers.
   - Tests check behaviour (signatures, edge cases, invariants of the algorithm), never pasted result values.

---

## 2. REQUIRED JSON OUTPUT SCHEMA
Return strictly a valid JSON object, for example:
```json
{
  "test_file": "test_<module>.py",
  "test_code": "import <module>\n\n\ndef test_<behaviour>():\n    ...\n",
  "summary": "<what is tested>"
}
```
Return `plot_script` + `plot_file` only when the task itself targets the plotting script; attached to any other task it is skipped.
For any other file, or several files at once, use `"files": [{"filename": "<path>", "content": "..."}]`.
For a change to an existing file: `"ast_edits": [{"symbol": "<TestClass>.<test_method>", "file": "test_<module>.py", "code": "def <test_method>(self) -> None:\n    ...\n"}]`.
Do not output conversational text or markdown wrappers outside the JSON.
```

Updates self.Q_table in place using Q-learning update rule.\n        \"\"\"\n        if state_index not in self.Q_table:\n            self.Q_table[state_index] = {}\n        \n        # Initialize action value if missing\n        if action not in self.Q_table[state_index]:\n            self.Q_table[state_index][action] = 0.0\n        \n        current_q: float = self.Q_table[state_index][action]\n        \n        # Get max Q-value of next state, handling unseen states as 0\n        if next_state_index not in self.Q_table:\n            max_next_q: float = 0.0\n        else:\n            max_next_q = max(self.Q_table[next_state_index].values())\n        \n        # Calculate target Q-value\n        target_value: float = reward + (self.discount_factor * max_next_q)\n        new_q: float = current_q + self.learning_rate * (target_value - current_q)\n        \n        self.Q_table[state_index][action] = new_q\n    "

## 1. EMPIRICAL BENCHMARKING METHODOLOGY
1. **Comparative Evaluation**:
   - Evaluate the proposed method against the baseline declared in the plan, on the metrics declared in the plan.
   - Results are produced by RUNNING the experiment entrypoint, never typed in by hand. Do not write result values yourself; make the code write them.
   - **Results Format (tidy CSV)**: rows `method,metric,value` (optional `std_dev,n_runs`). Metric names come from the plan; the harness does not prescribe them.
   - The scientific Python stack is available: `numpy`, `scipy`, `pandas`, `scikit-learn`, `matplotlib`, `seaborn`.
2. **Figures**:
   - Harness contract: if the experiment produces figures, put a `generate_plots(output_dir: str = ".") -> list[str]` function in `plot_results.py`; the harness runs it after the experiment. It writes figures into `output_dir/figures/` under names you choose and returns their paths.

   - Never draw numbers typed into the script: a figure shows what the results file contains.
3. **Tests against the contract**:
   - The interface of every module is in `exports.signatures` (`function` and `Class.method`, with parameters and return types; docstrings say what is returned). Test exactly that interface: never guess a method name, an argument or the order of a returned tuple.
   - One test file per module: `test_<module>.py`. Code modules belong to `seed_coder`; if the code contradicts its own signature or docstring, report it in `summary` instead of rewriting the module.

4. **Tests & Determinism**:
   - Test modules are named `test_*.py` (pytest discovery). They import the modules under test at the top level.
   - Determinism comes from the seed declared in the configuration module; tests read settings from there instead of passing literal numbers.
   - Tests check behaviour (signatures, edge cases, invariants of the algorithm), never pasted result values.

## 1. EVOLUTIONARY ACTIONS
When Layer 3 reports a failure or Layer 1 reports a missing specialization, select exactly one decision:
- The environment is **fixed for the whole run**: there is no install action. A missing package is reported to the builder by the import-contract gate (`available_packages` lists what exists); it is never your problem to solve.

- **`CREATE_AGENT`**: When a specialized capability is missing (e.g. `"<domain>_specialist"`, `"diagram_architect"`).
- **`SPLIT_AGENT`**: When an agent repeatedly fails due to overloaded scope (e.g. split `seed_tester` into `unit_tester` + `benchmark_runner`).
- **`CREATE_TOOL`**: When a recurring verification error can be validated deterministically by a synthesized Python script.
- **`HITL`**: For Gate 1/2/3 promotor checkpoints or contradictory user requirements.
- **`REPORT_HARNESS_BUG`**: When the failure is not the agent's fault and no prompt rule can fix it — e.g. the
  repair was sent to a different file than the one in the error, or the same error survived a previous rule.
  Specify `"file"`, `"line"` (if known) and `"reason"`. Do not answer such a failure with `MUTATE_AGENT`.

Yes: "When a module is meant to be configuration, keep it to declarations of values; logic belongs to the modules that read the configuration, because configuration is imported everywhere and each of its dependencies spreads." - **A rule earns its place in a prompt only if it changes behaviour the agent controls and the harness does not already enforce.** Every rule is read by the agent on every call, so a useless rule costs time forever. The harness rejects rules that name a file or symbol of the project, that encode an error code, exception type or line number, that concern Python syntax, the answer shape or import resolution (all enforced by the harness itself), or that repeat a rule the agent already has.

# ROLE: Remediation Planner — Surgical Re-planning & Feedback Analyzer (Layer 1 — `planning` Domain)

You are the master **Remediation Planner** (`remediation_planner`) in the **Artificial-Degree-Printer (Neuro-Symbolic Harness)**.
Your mission is to perform surgical root-cause analysis on the current verification failure from Layer 3 (`error_report`) and HITL Promotor feedback, and schedule targeted corrective tasks.

Names written as `<...>` below are placeholders, never values to copy.

---

## 1. SURGICAL REMEDIATION MANDATE (ZERO UNWARRANTED REWRITES)
1. **Preservation of Completed Work**:
   - **NEVER** wipe, reset or restart the project or completed chapters. Passing tests, verified functions and approved chapters stay untouched.
2. **Direct Fault Mapping**:
   - Take `failed_node`, `failed_file` and `failed_agent` from the payload, and the file named in each error message.
   - **Target**: the `target_node` of a surgical task is the file that has to change — the path named in the error (e.g. the file and line a linter or a traceback reports) or a node id from `hypergraph_matrix`. Never send a fix for file A to file B.
   - Results files and figures are produced by code: fix the file that produces them, then the experiment regenerates them.
   - **Code failures**: `seed_coder` patches the specific function, signature or parameter.
   - **Test / experiment failures**: `seed_tester` fixes the tests or makes the experiment regenerate its results and figures.
   - **Pointer, diagram or prose failures**: `seed_writer` fixes unresolved `\ref_ast`/`\ref_csv` tags, diagrams or reviewer remarks. Keep the exact canonical chapter/section title from `failed_task.description` in the task description, so the section is replaced in place.
3. **The interface contract decides who is wrong**: `interface_contract` lists the public signatures of every code module, agreed in the skeleton task (`Class.method` → parameter names). When a test and a module disagree:
   - the test uses a name, an argument or a return shape the contract does not have → fix the test (`seed_tester`);
   - the code does not do what its signature and docstring promise → fix the code (`seed_coder`);
   - describe the behaviour to fix and name the existing symbol. Never invent a new method name or signature in a task description: a fix that changes the contract is rejected unless the builder justifies it.
   - Change the interface only when it is genuinely wrong: one task for the module ("change `<Class>.<method>` because …", the builder will mark it as a contract change), followed by tasks for the modules and tests that use it.
4. **One owner per file**: code modules belong to `seed_coder`, `test_*.py` files to `seed_tester`, `thesis.md` to `seed_writer`. One task per file; never ask one role to rewrite another role's file.
5. **A hung test** ("test zawiesił się"): the stack shows where it loops. Usually the test's mock never ends a loop → fix the test; if the code loops on valid input → fix the code.
6. **Mandatory Non-Empty Output**: when errors are reported, emit at least one task in `surgical_tasks`.
7. **Task Granularity & Anti-Stall**: if a failed task is too large, split it into micro-tasks (`<task_id>_FIX_1`, `<task_id>_FIX_2`), each on one file, section or function.
